explanation: Fires on an interior connector token inside a multi-token fixed unit that is clearly going to continue: the decimal point in a number (10[.]4, XCode 3[.]1), hyphens inside chemical/gene/institution names (HLA[-]DRB3, COX[-]2, Philipps[-]Universität), and function words inside organisation names (Campaign [for] Real Ale, National Association for [the] Education). Ordinary prose connectors outside such names are weak.

Fires on a noun naming something that belongs to or comes from a preceding possessor or source: strongest for 'account' after 'an/your/player' ('you already have an account'), 'beam' after 'electron/laser', and 'eyes', 'name', 'voice', 'stories' after a possessive (her voice, his name, their stories). Generic nouns without an owner are weak.

Fires on a word-initial prefix piece of a word split into several tokens, above all ' micro' (microgravity, microcontroller, microarray, micro-organisms), and also 'ad' (adoration, adjudication, Advising), 'i' in 'i.e.', and 'Res'urrection. Whole-word tokens are weak.

Fires mostly on the first piece of a multi-token word or compound modifier, often right after 'a/the' (a [not]-for-profit, a [Devon] Rex, a [books]eller, [but]yl, [agar]ose, [Wasser]stein, [No]etherian), but also on assorted words like 'used', 'anything', 'moderately'. There is no single clear semantic theme.

Fires on a few specific nouns that head a phrase: 'truth' ('the truth is', 'further from the truth', Truthout), 'art' ('art director', 'the art of', 'Art Center'), 'life' in 'battery life', and 'control'/'management' in software compounds (access control, session management). Other nouns are weak.

Fires inside license/copyright boilerplate in source-code header comments: 'License' in 'limitations under the License', 'reserved' in 'All rights reserved', and periods or comment markers in auto-generated-code notices. The strongest case is the period in the C# AssemblyInfo comment 'controlled through the following set of attributes.' It is near-silent outside code headers.

Fires on a token that completes a well-known identifier or proper name: library/API names in code (timedelta, .hibernate, .intellij, WebClient, Object.defineProperty, UIControl, getJSON, tbody) and familiar names (Christie, Whatsapp, Brexit, San Diego), plus a few odd words (condolence, reputations, stash). It is a mixture.

Fires weakly to moderately on scattered tokens: CJK characters and full-width punctuation, digits in numbers or ranges, slashes in URLs and paths, code tokens such as '<' and 'y', and closing parentheses. No consistent context.

A mixture: 'the' after won/received when an award or championship follows (won the PBA National Championship), pieces of personal names (Neymar, Toussaint, Nygard, Niels), spaces before years and distances in event names, and Objective-C/Swift/build-file code tokens (canImport, WithException, }/). Other tokens are scattered.

Fires on tokens inside non-English or byte-garbled text (Japanese/Chinese characters, broken UTF-8 bytes, Devanagari, mid-word pieces of German or transliterated names like Shaoyun, Solanum) and on zeros inside long runs of zeros. English prose words are weak.

Fires mostly in technical/scientific method text on a connector or modifier inside a method or term name ('Univariate [and] multivariate', 'parametric [and] non-parametric', '[root] mean square', 'region [of] interest', '[small] interfering RNA'), and also on file-format and code tokens (.asc, typedef, Rich Text Format, -gdwarf). A loose mixture.

Fires on words that express wondering or uncertainty and introduce an indirect question: 'wondering/wondered/wonder' (strongest in 'I am wondering if/whether'), plus 'confused as [to]', 'puzzling [over]', 'unsure', 'the question remains/is'. It is weaker on other question words ('how', 'what') and silent elsewhere.

Fires on assorted tokens, mostly in code (#include, #define, extractData, logLevel, \frac, operators like '+' and '<<') and on legal-opinion headers ('Circuit Judges.'), plus scattered prose words (her, never, cannot, female). No unifying theme.

Fires on the modifier word of a technical compound noun, typically right before its head (metal oxide, GO train, neural tube, side platform, wireless device, cognitive vigilance, Methodist Hospital, fee-for-service), and also on Chinese/Japanese characters in localization strings and on numbers or parentheses in statistics. A mixture, with the technical-compound modifier as the most common case.
